articles.title: Emergency matters
articles.content: THE new setup in KP is taking shape rapidly and quietly. While everyone seems focused on the collective meltdown in the PTI, the province the party ruled until recently is busy setting up a new structure. The governor announced his newadvisory councilwithin days, while the emergency-stricken districts have been provided with their own administrative machinery. A special emergency has been declared in the former Fata regions as well as Bannu, Lakki Marwat, Tank, and Dera Ismail Khan. According to the information available in news reports, these regions will now be managed by a new Area Development Secretariat (ADS), which is to be headed by a bureaucrat, Yahya Akhundzada, an additional chief secretary (ACS). It is being reported that he has been given extensive powers akin to those of a cabinet or a provincial government. Along with this, a new council has been formed, consisting of four people from each district to assist him. An additional inspector general (AIG) of police is also part of this council. Most of these members have been selected, with a few refusals; not bad for a week’s worth of work. At the federal level, a committeeheadedby Ishaq Dar has been formed to supervise the province. Besides Dar, the committee includes several PML-N stalwarts, mostly from Punjab, such as Rana Sanaullah, Azam Nazeer Tarar, and Attaullah Tarar. However, other members include Amir Muqam from KP and Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui from Karachi. At times, the plan appears more ambitious than merely addressing terrorism and governance in KP. In the past week, whispers have been heard around Islamabad; well-informed journalists have also appeared on television and suggested that this setup might decide the future of the other provinces as well. If the technocratic cabinets are able to perform well, there is a chance similar setups may be introduced elsewhere. Faisal Vawda, who, too, has much inside news to share, has suggested or hinted at something similar. This is lent credence by the manner in which the new administration has been installed in KP, where governor’s rule is accompanied by a special setup for the 12 districts; if there were ever to be smaller provinces in the country, these districts could easily take the form of a ‘South Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’ province. At times, the plan appears more ambitious than merely addressing terrorism and governance in KP. Be that as it may, all these ambitious plans — if there are any — will have to wait until the wrinkles are ironed out in KP. I say this because, from the outside, there seems to be a lack of clarity at the moment. There is some confusion about how this new setup will work. After all, not only is there a governor now in charge of the province, but there is also a powerful ADS for southern KP. So, will the ADS report to the governor or directly to the federal government? That is a bit unclear at the moment. This also raises the question of what the ADS’s relationship will be with the provincial bureaucracy. If the ACS and AIG report directly to Islamabad, will this eliminate the need to work with Peshawar entirely? Journalists from the province say the ADS and the federal government will handle development and security directly. This is why the ADS, according to one colleague, is even being given its own set of finance and planning officials. These officials will be part of the new secretariat. But what will happen in matters that do not fall under development and security, such as education and health? That is why some feel that, for the moment, there may still be a need to coordinate with the provincial bureaucracy and thrash out other issues. And if that is the case, it can cause delays and hurdles. After all, red tape and bureaucratic hurdles are routine in the country, but if, in this case, rules need to be figured out or made anew, the delays might be more severe. In addition, as mentioned earlier, there is confusion over how many issues in this special region will go directly to the prime minister or the provincial setup/governor before being routed to the prime minister. While journalists from KP feel the prime minister and Islamabad will deal with all matters directly, the ADR spokesman said in a television interview that the prime minister would handle issues in which the governor and his team could not address the needs of the 12 districts. If the prime minister, or rather the federal government, is to look after every issue, will decision-making power go to the Dar-led committee? It is hard to imagine that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will have the time to look into every matter individually. The prime minister also prefers to manage matters through committees. But how efficient will this prove to be? Of course, the assumption is that decision-making will be quick and efficient because it will take place elsewhere, and the committees we see exist in name only. No doubt, this is always a possibility, but how many governance issues can be managed this way? Development and security decisions can perhaps be handled in this manner, but will there be no other issues? Though one should remain optimistic, I suppose. However, let me venture to say that if this new technocratic setup proves to be successful and efficient, it might just end up increasing centralisation of decision-making, which is far removed from the idea of local government and service delivery at the people’s doorstep. For residents of the 12 districts, Islamabad and cities beyond are much farther away than Peshawar.
articles.author: Arifa Noor

articles.title: Every runner in the race
articles.content: IN a relay race, one must trust all running partners equally, and not second-guess the other’s abilities or overestimate one’s own ability to deliver victory or gain glory. That would be a different field of activity and not the race in which the baton is passed at the quickest possible speed. Worryingly, the movement against the mass rigging of elections in India is beginning to look like a relay race in which the runners are not necessarily looking together at the end of the linear, or oval, or meandering track ahead. In some tellings, the challenge is trickier, more like a trapeze act, and without a safety net. A miss of the clap of the partner’s hands or misjudging the timing of a leap could lead to injury or worse. No matter how equipped one party feels about its own sinews to carry the baton to the finish line by itself, a collective race offers no quarter to one-upmanship. If the objective is to bring down the Modi government, which is what Congress and its supporters say they hope to do, there is an absence of team coordination. A clear discussion is required with all stakeholders for a shared understanding of the game plan. Call it a common minimum programme, if you like. If the objective is to clean up governance, which is what the Cockroach group has committed itself to from the start — a transparent, humane judiciary, an independent corporate-free media, accountable bureaucracy, a trustworthy election commission, a truly representative parliament with 50 per cent women MPs — all these objectives are also ways of reaching the same outcome: the desire for the dismantling of a right-wing regime. Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s reported comments that his party is aiming for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and that it doesn’t share the enthusiasm for regime change, need to be parsed and accepted with empathy. The youngsters may not have built the appetite for prison visits or the daily brutal assaults by police and state-run goons. Besides, they may genuinely fear their agenda was being hijacked by allies with larger resources or experience in the field. Nearly everyone opposed to the Modi government is overlooking the acumen needed to learn from history. There could be nothing truly wrong with a call to change the Modi regime. Modi has similarly called for removing Manmohan Singh, and the JP movement was all about overthrowing Indira Gandhi’s government. In which case, everyone should be made aware of what is involved in the effort and whether they all feel equipped to bear the inevitable pushback from the regime they seek to dismantle. There is already an undeclared emergency. If push comes to shove, the government has the wherewithal to formally suspend civil liberties. The BJP echo chamber has been describing the campaign against vote theft as a leftist conspiracy. It may not be a coincidence that the government has timed a verbal exchange with China over India’s curiously announced renaming of certain places in Ladakh at the height of the Delhi protests. The timing coincided with an evolving attack on communist parties that have participated with full strength in the protests. The bulldozer attacks on communist book stalls in BJP-ruled West Bengal during the ongoing Durga puja celebrations offer a clue to this plan. The one obstacle that comes to mind against an open declaration of emergency is not one from the activists. It could come, instead, from the RSS, the fountainhead of the Hindutva fold, which wouldn’t want to hand over any extra powers itself to any prime minister or his cabinet. Anyone familiar with the history of the Third Reich would know of the swiftness with which the Führer eliminated the leadership of the SA in what is remembered as the Night of the Long Knives. In that fear lies a potential deterrent to a formal clampdown, though the right-wing state has equipped itself with all manner of underhand methods to keep a truly mortal challenge at bay. Nearly everyone opposed to the Modi government is overlooking the acumen needed to learn from history. The last time an entrenched fascist party was removed from power, it needed a world war and an unconscionable toll of human lives. In a more recent and relatively local context, it took the so-called champions of global democracy 20 years of war and trillions of dollars in treasure and human lives to replace the Taliban with the Taliban. If we align the world’s three most implacable right-wing ducks in a row — Donald Trump, Benjamin Netanyahu, and Narendra Modi — the most organised to fend off dethronement should be the Indian duck, followed by the Israeli and the American. Of the three, the orange-haired goose, although the most powerful of the three, looks the readiest to be cooked (or impeached) after the midterms. Netanyahu needs a miracle to survive by defeating Iran. And since that is not going to happen, he may be plotting something equally kinetic to cancel the election. Modi needs to do nothing of the sort. The required first step to restore a functional democracy in India is for the current regime to go. Would it go the same way as another regime was shown the door in 1977? Extremely unlikely. Today is not 1977 and Narendra Modi is not Indira Gandhi. The West opposed her short-lived dictatorship not for the love of democracy but because she was a mainstay of the Soviet camp during the Cold War. Modi became prime minister as a consensus candidate for India’s big businesses, with their comprador levers abroad. Like the Israeli lobby in the US, they too ply their MPs. Modi can be removed if the consensus switches sides. But that brings the status quo, not change. The Cockroaches, Congress, and every runner in the fray have just one choice — to plan to win the relay race, to defeat the quarry instead of bickering over the baton. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi.
articles.author: Jawed Naqvi

articles.title: School collapse
articles.content: THE recent collapse of a school building in Peshawar’s Dir Colony, which killed over 30 students and left many injured, should serve as a wake-up call for the authorities. Whether officials will finally take long-term action to prevent such tragedies is not known at the moment. True, the authorities are quick to take ‘remedial measures’ in the wake of a disaster, but the action hardly has the desired effect. The National Disaster Management Authority, alongside its provincial and district counterparts, was created after the 2005 earthquake in KP and Azad Kashmir. An Earthquake Reconstruction and Rehabilitation Authority was also created and later merged with the NDMA. However, in several instances, the NDMA has failed to live up to its mandate. In the case of Peshawar, as in other Pakistani cities, various agencies have the mandate to regulate building practices in their jurisdictions. Development authorities, municipal corporations, provincial land-use and building-control authorities, and school monitoring regulators share responsibility. But tragedies like the recent school collapse still happen. School managements must be advised to have their premises assessed for building safety. Ideally, a team of professional engineers and architects should do this. However, many school managements find their services costly. To reduce extraneous costs, a simple inventory list can be prepared by a senior teacher covering the age of the building and its various constituent spaces; visible defects in the structure, furniture and fixtures; status of electricity wiring, boards, hanging wires, cables, ceiling fans and lighting fixtures; location of gas installations, emergency exits (if any); location and safety of the water supply infrastructure; quality of school flooring, pavements and stairs; physical barriers and potential hazards; and storage spaces. The school’s immediate surroundings must also be assessed, as open gutters, hanging electrical wiring, broken roads, public junkyards, etc, can harm students and staff. School managements must then prepare a priority list of actions. Implementation comes first. In government schools especially, it may take a lot of effort to get the principal to carry out any evaluation, which they may consider beyond their assigned responsibilities. Here, parental pressure will help. If there is a parent-teacher association, the task is easier. Where the cost is small, the school’s imprest funds can cover it. For larger expenses, the relevant authority can be approached — with follow-up pressure, since bureaucracy can take a while to swing into action. Safety audits must be conducted in all schools. Private schools should use a different, more tailored strategy. Established chains may already be in touch with architects and engineers who can carry out a survey. Medium-tier schools can also approach qualified professionals — the costs may not be that high at the investigation stage. Similarly, private schools in lower-income localities may be asked to approach the relevant NGOs and professional bodies (for example, the Institution of Engineers or the Institute of Architects) for assistance. In many cases, reaching out has worked well. At a minimum, professional bodies can be asked to train some of the teaching staff to identify hazards and implement safety plans. Most private schools operate in rented residences. Overcrowded classrooms and shoddily constructed premises, along with schools’ locations on busy urban roads, must be addressed through policy. Building and zoning regulators often disregard construction violations. At times, these risks become larger hazards, such as stampedes during emergency evacuations. Unfortu-nately, civic authorities do not prioritise allocating plots for educational purposes in planned neighbourhoods. School managements’ inability to acquire land at affordable prices is a serious obstacle to building proper schools. Since the neighbourhoods attract students from across the city, hapless pupils can be seen crossing the streets on which badly driven vehicles endanger their lives. This hazard alone should compel city authorities to take firm and lasting action. KP’s interim administration should consider establishing a steering committee, chaired by an independent technocrat, to take the necessary measures to make school buildings safe across Peshawar. The committee must comprise architects, engineers, academics, civil society members, representatives of relevant government bodies and departments and social mobilisers, and should carry out the tasks needed to ensure positive reform. The writer is an academic and researcher based in Karachi.
articles.author: Dr Noman Ahmed

articles.title: Trump & Pakistan
articles.content: WRITING about Pakistan-US ties is like penning literary criticism of a Shakespearean play. One constantly reinterprets and looks for new answers to old questions. How does one evaluate Pak-US ties under President Donald Trump? Do Trump’s extravagant compliments to Pakistan’s leadership reflect happy relations between the two countries? The short answer is no. American leaders routinely indulge in hyperbole. Add to it the sales pitch of a marketing ‘genius’, and you get Trump’s effusive but effervescent compliments. Compared to Joe Biden’s time, US-Pakistan ties have no doubt been elevated, but not upgraded. The uptick stems from more than Trump’s bonhomie with Pakistan’s leadership. The relationship is largely a function of his experimental foreign policy. He is reassessing America’s China policy and relations with Russia, rebalancing ties with traditional allies and partners — to America’s advantage — and deprioritising, though not abandoning, the traditional foreign policy establishment’s overweening ambitions to maintain US global primacy. The emphasis is on unilateralism, the naked use of military power, and economic warfare. This foreign policy stems from his whims, with his politics oriented towards the MAGA movement and the rich class, especially tech billionaires; tariffs used as leverage not only for trade but also for geopolitical gain; and a search for greater market share for America, as well as potential investment and business deals with China and Russia. Pakistan has been an incidental beneficiary of Trump’s policies, good or bad. It has again tried to play its historical role of rescuer in America’s adventures. It has gained by dramatically enhancing itsdiplomatic profilein the Middle East and its image in America. Washington appears to appreciate the need to maintain Pakistan’s defence capability for regional stability, especially in South Asia, and to use it as leverage against India. Pakistan, a populous country and a nuclear power, occupies an important geostrategic position between the subcontinent, Iran, Arabia, Central Asia, Russia, and China. Its strength is an asset, and its weakness a liability. One makes it a useful partner; the other makes it hard to ignore, much less alienate. Washington wants to contain China’s political and economic profile in Pakistan. Alienating it would shut the door on all US influence. The US benefits from a tangible relationship with Pakistan. America benefits from a tangible relationship with Pakistan in various areas of cooperation. The Trump administrationapproveda $686 million upgrade and sustainment package for Pakistan’s F-16 fleet. Separately, a $488m foreign military sales contract wasawardedto Northrop Grumman for APG-66 and APG-68 radar engineering and technical support, covering 21 countries, including Pakistan. Pak-US cooperation is also developing in the economic area, mainly in energy, IT, crypto, agriculture, renewable energy, and critical minerals, where Pakistan is drawing attention as a significant source. America is also the top destination for Pakistan’s exports. The US needs Pakistan’s cooperation to act against transnational terrorists who endanger regional, American, and global security. Counterterrorism cooperation thus continues. Lastly, Washington has always been concerned about a Pakistan-India conflict and will continue to play a crisis management role. Behind the veneer of Trump’s rhetoric and personalised foreign policy, however, traditional foreign policy seems to be at work, led by China hawk and pro-India Secretary of State Marco Rubio, which may be circumscribing Pak-US ties. Otherwise, how do we explain that neither he, nor the deputy secretary, nor an under-secretary of state has visited Pakistan? There’s no semblance of a strategic relationship, despite Rubio’s lip service to the idea. So, is Trump pursuing a dual-track policy, especially regarding the China policy and its derivative India policy, that influences the administration’s approach to Pakistan? Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent hinted at the ‘real’ China policy when he said in an interview that the relationship with China poses an unprecedented national security challenge. “China is … the biggest economic threat, and they’re the biggest military threat,” he said. The reality is that Trump hasn’t done anything extraordinary for Pakistan that we might fear losing. Much of his freelance foreign policy will likely depart with him, but the impact on Pak-US ties might be minimal. US-Israeli wars in the Middle East have dented America’s standing in the region, providing a fresh rationale for continued engagement with Pakistan in the post-Trump world. Bottom line: The relationship with the US is necessary but not indispensable. We should keep it that way to safeguard our strategic autonomy.
articles.author: Touqir Hussain

articles.title: Burnt bridges
articles.content: A WEEK after the federal governmentimposedgovernor’s rule and emergency in KP, PPP Chairperson Bilawal Bhutto-Zardariinvitedthe opposition to engage ‘positively’ with the centre, saying this could lead to their reversal. Mr Bhutto-Zardari, addressing reporters at a Sunday memorial for the 2007 Karsaz attack on his late mother Benazir Bhutto’s homecoming procession, spoke about the need for a national effort to address the growing economic crisis, resurgent terrorism, and Pakistan’s increasingly dysfunctional electoral system. But his offer, however well-meaning, stands little chance of leading to a political breakthrough in the current climate. Without concrete confidence-building measures initiated by the ruling parties, the opposition is unlikely to put much faith in mere assurances, given that the centre has crossed a major political red line by deposing an elected provincial government and supplanting it with a setup handpicked by Islamabad. Mr Bhutto-Zardari seemed to be missing the point when he called the ‘non-functional’ KP chief minister a “coward” who was “not ready to defend his own land”. Whatever his failings, the people of KP had elected him, and the remedy lay with them, not with Islamabad. By forcing him aside, the centre has signalled that it does not need public consensus to do as it pleases. The centre’s dispute with KP, after all, was not about whether terrorism needed confronting, but how. KP had resisted the centre’s approach to fighting terrorism, and the resulting stand-off had stymied any progress. In dismissing the provincial government, the centre had signalled that security policies would be prescribed for the province rather than derived in consultation with it. That bridge has already been burnt. It is commendable that the PPP chairperson is at least talking about a path back to normalcy, but the PPP is a partner in the very government that imposed governor’s rule. If it wants the decision reversed, it should convince its ally in Islamabad, not ask the opposition to be ‘positive’. It is hoped that the PML-N will also reconsider its position. The latter party would do well to recall that, in 2009, when its government in Punjab was dismissed and governor’s rule imposed, it had itself joined a ‘long march’ on Islamabad to press its demands. It is unbecoming of that party to have denied its opponents the same right to protest now, when it is in power. It will not be easy to build bridges with the opposition, but the PML-N, more than any other party, has the power to concede some ground to show goodwill. It should take up the National Assembly opposition leader on his offer to engage the jailed PTI chief, and facilitate that effort if it is serious about national reconciliation and a unified response to Pakistan’s crises.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Toll on trade
articles.content: A YEAR after Islamabad severed commercial ties with Kabul over security concerns, the border trade disruption is taking a growing toll on KP, where livelihoods, businesses, farm markets, and a large number of workers depend on cross-border commerce. Bilateral trade has fallen by more than 72pc, from $1.3bn in FY25 to $358m in FY26 — which means fewer customers for local shops, lower earnings for farmers, idle trucks, and lost jobs. KP was already struggling to attract investment and create work amid rising terrorism; the loss of an established market makes recovery harder. The damage is not confined to the province. Farmers and factories in Punjab and Sindh, too, have been hit, and Pakistan’s exports to Central Asia have been badly disrupted. Afghanistan has long been KP’s natural outlet because of its proximity and the long-standing commercial and tribal networks. Traders built their businesses around moving food, cement, pharmaceuticals, and other goods across the border. Medical tourism, hotels, and other services catering to Afghan visitors are suffering as well. When crossings shut, traders cannot send their goods to distant markets without facing higher costs, finding new buyers, and adapting to unfamiliar commercial conditions. In fact, most services cannot be shifted at all. Rerouting shipments is not an easy fix. Pakistan’s shortest land routes to Central Asia run through Afghanistan. Alternatives mean longer distances, higher freight costs, and thinner margins. Small enterprises with little financial cushion are the most exposed to prolonged border trade closures. KP needs expanding markets and productive investment to employ a growing workforce; it cannot afford to lose existing ones before alternatives are in place. Islamabad has valid security concerns — the Taliban must prevent Afghan territory from being used for attacks on Pakistan. But border closures also hurt citizens on both sides, who have nothing to do with Kabul’s policies. Islamabad must find the right balance between its security priorities and the economic strain on KP’s residents. Sustained efforts to obtain genuine security assurances from Kabul and carefully monitored arrangements for legitimate trade may offer a way to protect both. It should also assess the losses of traders, transporters, and farmers, and help businesses find new markets. The government must protect its people from terrorism without restricting their livelihoods.
articles.author: Editorial
